## What this session covers

Most schools responded to generative AI by buying a detector and writing a policy that
points at it. This session argues that both halves of that response are weaker than they
look, and that the second one can be fixed. We'll work through what detection tools
actually measure, who gets caught by them and who doesn't, and how to write a
responsible-use policy that survives contact with a real classroom.

Bring a policy if you have one (your school's, your department's, or your own syllabus
language). You'll get time to mark it up.

## Session outline

| Time | Segment |
|-----:|:--------|
| ~10 min | What detection tools actually do |
| ~20 min | Who false positives land on |
| ~15 min | Writing a policy you can defend |

## Key points

- Detection tools don't detect AI. They estimate how statistically unsurprising a piece of
  writing is, which is a different thing.
- Tested against a 2015 dissertation and a paragraph written by a language model this
  month, a commercial detector called both of them human.
- Where these tools do err, the errors have historically fallen hardest on the students
  least able to absorb the cost of being wrongly accused.
- A policy that makes detector output the evidence has outsourced an academic-integrity
  judgment to a vendor.
- What holds up is writing permitted use into the assignment, in terms of what the
  assignment is trying to teach.

## The detection problem

### Two documents

I ran a test the week before this workshop, and the result is why this session exists in
its current form.

The first document was a section of the literature review from my own doctoral
dissertation. I wrote it in 2015. There was no large language model available to write it
with, so whatever else is true of that text, it can't contain AI-generated prose.

The second was a paragraph a language model wrote at my direction on the morning of July
27, 2026. I asked it to restate a passage of the same dissertation in plainer language.
It's machine-generated in the most straightforward sense available.

I put both through commercial AI detectors.

| Document | Provenance | GPTZero (model 4.7b) | ZeroGPT | Copyleaks |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Dissertation literature review, 1,779 words | Human, 2015 | 100% human | 0.6% AI | 0% AI |
| Restated paragraph, 334 words | LLM, July 2026 | 100% human | 0% AI | *not yet run* |

One of those documents couldn't have been written by a machine. The other couldn't have
been written by anything else. Both tools called both of them human. GPTZero used the same
words each time: *"We are highly confident this text is entirely human."* Not a hedge, not
a maybe. The phrasing a teacher would act on.

Now look at the ordering. ZeroGPT scored the 2015 dissertation at 0.6% AI and the
machine-written paragraph at 0%. It didn't just fail to tell them apart. It ranked them
backwards. The one document in the pair that could not possibly contain AI-generated prose
is the one it found marginally more suspicious.

The margin is small enough that neither text would be flagged by any sane threshold, and
that's the point. A weak signal you can compensate for by moving the cutoff. An
arbitrary ordering leaves you nothing to move.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Two caveats, since someone will ask

The dissertation was run on GPTZero's Advanced scan and the paragraph on its Basic scan
(the free tier allows one Advanced scan per day). The two documents also differ
substantially in length. So two variables moved, not one, and this is a demonstration
rather than an experiment.

Note which way the length difference cuts, though. Shorter text gives a detector less to
work with, which should make the machine-written paragraph the *harder* case. It was still
called human with high confidence. The confound runs against the tool, not in its favor.
:::

### What the tool measures

This isn't a malfunction. A detector doesn't recognize machine authorship, because machine
authorship leaves no signature to recognize. What it measures is predictability, roughly
how closely word choice tracks what a language model would have chosen next. That's a
proxy, and the gap between the proxy and the thing it stands for is where every one of
these results lives.

Two things follow that a better version doesn't fix.

The first is that the signal is weakest where the stakes are highest. A short assignment
gives the tool less to work with than a long one, so the scores that matter most in a
middle-school classroom are the least reliable ones. OpenAI withdrew its own classifier in
2023 on the grounds that accuracy was too low to be useful. A company with every
commercial reason to keep it running concluded it couldn't.

The second is the base rate, and it's the part people skip. Suppose a tool is right most of
the time, and most students in a class of thirty didn't use AI. A meaningful share of the
flags it raises will still be wrong. The number a vendor quotes is accuracy on their own
test set. The number that matters to you is the chance that *this* flagged student actually
did it, and that number is lower, sometimes much lower. That's the difference between a
tool that identifies cheating and a tool that generates a list of students to go and
accuse.

### Why they now under-flag

There's a further wrinkle, and it explains the table above. After the false-positive
research of 2023 and the press that followed it, vendors recalibrated toward not accusing
people. Several now market low false-positive rates as a feature.

That's the right direction to have moved in. But a detector tuned to almost never accuse
falsely is also a detector that almost never catches anything. The trade was sensitivity for
safety, and it shifted the worry. Wrongful accusation was the 2023 problem. The 2026 problem
is that the tool may be doing nothing for you at all.

## Equity

When these tools do get it wrong, the errors aren't distributed evenly.

Liang and colleagues ran a set of widely used GPT detectors against writing by native and
non-native English speakers. The detectors classified the native-speaker samples almost
perfectly. They misclassified **more than half** of the non-native samples as AI-generated.

Two things about that study matter for how much weight to put on it. It's strong evidence,
published, replicated in its own design, mechanistically explained. And it's from 2023, run
against the detectors of that moment. The recalibration described above happened partly
*because* of findings like this one. So treat it as evidence about what these tools do when
they're tuned to catch things, rather than as a current measurement of any particular
product.

The mechanism is the part that outlives the vintage. When the researchers enriched the
vocabulary in the non-native samples, the misclassification rate fell. When they simplified
the native-speaker samples, it rose. The tools are reading lexical range as evidence of
humanity, so they penalize a limited English vocabulary and reward a large one, which is a
proxy for the thing schools are supposed to be teaching rather than punishing.

Follow that through to the students in front of you. An English learner writes plainly
because they're still acquiring the language. A student using assistive or predictive
writing technology under an IEP produces smoothed, conventional prose by design. A student
who's been taught to write to a formula writes to the formula. Each of these is a student
doing the thing we asked, and each of them is likelier to be flagged than a confident
writer who never had to think about it.

Meanwhile the students who can pay for the better tools are also the students likelier to
produce the idiosyncratic prose that reads as human. The tool sorts partly on advantage.

Then consider what an accusation costs. It costs a confident student one uncomfortable
conversation. It costs a student who's already unsure whether they belong considerably
more, and some of them don't come back from it.

## Writing a responsible-use policy

The practical half. A policy is doing its job when a student can tell, before starting,
what they're allowed to do, and when you can act on a suspicion without a detector score
being your only evidence.

Four things make the difference.

### Set the rule per assignment, not per course

Blanket bans fail because they aren't believed and aren't enforceable. Blanket permission
fails because it doesn't distinguish between tasks. Whether AI use is acceptable depends on
what the specific task is meant to develop, and brainstorming and final prose aren't the
same question.

### Say what the assignment is for

"You may not use AI" invites lawyering. "This assignment exists so you practice building an
argument from sources, so the argument and the prose need to be yours. Use AI to check your
grammar afterwards if you like." That version tells the student what's actually being
protected, and it holds up when they ask why.

### Define disclosure concretely

Name where it goes, what it says, and how long it should be. A one-line note at the end of
the document, saying what tool was used and for what, is enough. Unenforced disclosure
requirements just teach students that the rules are decorative.

### Separate suspicion from evidence

Decide in advance what you do when something looks off, and make the first step a
conversation rather than a charge. Ask the student to talk you through their drafting. That
conversation is more diagnostic than any score, and it's survivable when you turn out to be
wrong. Which you sometimes will be.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Takeaway

Write the rule into the assignment, not into the detector. A policy that explains what the
work is *for* gives students something they can follow and gives you something you can
defend. A policy that rests on a similarity score gives you neither.
:::
